name: Fitness Story NW
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, and that pack is the one to read
first: the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the
transcription, the rewrite, the block at the foot of the frame and
every number in it are the same and are named here rather than
restated. What makes this show itself is one sentence long - it is set
in Century Gothic Bold, in one cream, on the photograph itself with no
card under it and with no highlight - and everything below is that
sentence.
The NW in the name is the account's, the way the DE is in Fitness
Story DE and the NW in Crowned Ladies NW: it says which of the brand's
feeds this is and not what language the app is in. What lands on the
frames is whatever the video's own voice track was saying, put through
the transcription and the rewrite exactly as on every channel here;
nothing in this pack changes that, and everything the app itself says
is English like the rest of it (see CLAUDE.md).
It shares a brand with Fitness Story and Fitness Story DE and shares
almost no design with either, which is worth saying out loud because
the three folders sort next to each other and somebody will assume one
was copied from another. Those two are Hall of Femme's card: a
coloured slab at the foot of the frame, a palette of four colours
handed to the user for the type and four more for the slab, and a
picked word that changes CUT. This one keeps the block where they put
it and drops all three - no card, no palette, no highlight - which is
as far as two packs under one heading go.
Written as its own folder rather than as an override of its siblings,
for the reason content/README.md gives: a channel is a folder that
gets dropped in. The prose below therefore points at hall-of-femme and
at crowned-ladies-fr wherever the reasoning is the same, and states
its own only where this pack actually decides something.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report.
Stated as a reference and not as numbers, because this channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not - and a pack
that restates a shared answer is a pack that can be missing a piece of
it. That is not hypothetical: channels arrived under this heading
captioning their frames with the transcript as spoken, because the
folder they were copied from predated `rewrite`.

_comment_title: What separates this show from the others under the heading: it is set
in Century Gothic Bold, in one cream, straight onto the PHOTOGRAPH
with no card behind it, and every line of every caption is set the
same way.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
freeform text box, where the block stands on the frame, the drag - is
the Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states what makes it
this show, and then states the two keys the missing card forces:
`shadow`, which has to come back, and `panel`, which has to be said out
loud to go away.
Century Gothic is a geometric sans built on circles - Monotype's
answer to ITC Avant Garde - and the Bold is the weight that lets it
stand on a photograph without a card under it. That is the whole
argument for the cut rather than the Regular: a 400-weight geometric
has thin joins where the circles meet the stems, and a thin join is
the first thing a busy still eats. At 700 the stems are even and heavy
the whole way round, which is the same property that makes the face a
signage face.
It is also WIDE, which is the one thing to know before writing for it
and is measured in content/faces/century-gothic-bold.json rather than
here: twenty capitals can run past the 486px a line has, so the
occasional round sentence breaks at nineteen characters instead of the
preset's twenty. The wrapper does that on its own and nobody sees it
(see the two ceilings in js/caption.js) - it is noted because a caption
here takes a line more often than the same sentence on a narrower
sibling, and four lines is what the block is written to.
Uppercased, inherited, for the reason every one of its neighbours is:
at 40px with twenty characters to a line the caption is three short
beats rather than a paragraph, and capitals are what those are set in.
It costs nothing here - a geometric sans is a face whose capitals are
the circles and the straight lines it was drawn from, and this one's
round O and pointed A are what it is recognised by.

_comment_color: A cream, and it is the whole palette rather than the first of
several: this show is set in one colour. It is therefore also what
every frame is drawn in, since a frame stores no colour of its own
until it is given one and there is no swatch here to give it one
with (see state.textColorFor).
#FEEECA is a warm off-white and not a white, and on a channel with
no card that is a decision about the photograph rather than about
the brand palette. A caption with no ground under it is separated
from the picture by two things only - its colour and its shadow -
and against skin, hair and daylight, which is what these stills
are, a pure white is the one light colour that turns up in the
picture as well: a blown highlight, a white wall, a studio
backdrop. A cream sits just off all of them.
Which frame is the risky one follows from where the colour sits.
Its relative luminance is about 0.86, so it stands 18 times clear
of a black and only 1.15 times clear of a white - a night still
holds it with room to spare and a blown, sunlit one is where it
disappears entirely. That is the still the shadow below is chosen
for, and it is why the shadow is a dark one. It is the opposite
end of the range from Crowned Ladies FR's magenta, which is in
trouble at the light end too but has some tone of its own to fall
back on; this colour has none, and leans on the shadow harder than
any caption under this heading.
_comment_colors: Absent, and that is the palette being stated rather than
forgotten. Hall of Femme, the pack this is cut from, offers rows
of swatches because its look IS the pairing - which of its colours
is the card and which is the type - and Fitness Story and Fitness
Story DE carry that over with palettes of their own. This show has
one colour and no card, so there is no pairing to offer and
nothing for a second button to be.
Left unstated rather than written as a list of one, which is the
answer Inkjection FR and Crowned Ladies FR both reached in the
same position: a row of one swatch is a control that cannot change
anything - it draws the colour already on screen, marked as
chosen, and clicking it does nothing a user can see. That is the
one kind of control this panel does not have anywhere (see the
note on `alignable` in js/editor.js). With no list the whole block
of colour rows is hidden instead - see editor.paletteOf, which
hides a row whose colours have nothing to recolour, and
renderColorButtons, which drops the block when no row survives.
Nothing counts these lists, so the day this show wants a second
colour it is one key in this file and the row appears.
_comment_shadow: An exception to the preset, and the first of the two keys the
missing card forces.
The preset states no shadow, and its reasoning is exact: there is a
solid slab under those letters in a colour the user picked, it
separates them from the photograph completely, and a shadow as well
would only smear the inside of the card. Take the card away and
every word of that stops being true - these letters are on a
photograph, with grain and edges and whatever was behind the
subject running through them.
A DARK shadow, and on this colour it is not a close call the way it
is for the other two cardless captions under this heading. Crowned
Ladies FR weighs a mid-tone magenta and Inkjection FR carries a
white halo because its navy is nearly black. A cream at 0.86
luminance is a light colour with nothing behind it: black is the
only side of it there is contrast on, so the shadow is the whole of
what holds it off a bright still.
The numbers are the skeleton's own (see BASE_TITLE_STYLE.shadow in
js/channels.js) rather than a fresh set invented here. They are
what every channel in this app that sets light type on a
photograph uses, which is the same job this is; a pack with no
reason of its own should not carry a number it merely agrees with,
and where it has to state one anyway it should state the one
already in use.
_comment_highlight: None. Every line of every caption on this channel is set the same
way, and the highlight buttons stand where they stand everywhere
else and go dead with a tooltip saying whose decision that was (see
editor.renderHlButtons). A brand whose lines are all one treatment
says so here rather than being given a highlight nobody could tell
apart from the type - see `highlight` in js/channels.js.
All three things a highlight could be are unavailable to this show,
and they run out in order. A change of CUT is what most of this
heading picks its words out with - both of this show's own siblings
included, which spend the two ends of a weight axis on it - and the
app carries one cut of Century Gothic; asking for a second weight
of it would be the browser emboldening or thinning the one file
there is, and a synthesised weight is measured as well as drawn. A
recolour needs a second colour, and this show has one. And a box
needs a fill, which would be a second colour again - and a graphic
in a frame whose whole design is type lying directly on the
picture.
Written as null rather than left out, for the reason `panel` below
is: `use` merges the preset UNDER this pack (see `expand` in
js/channels.js), so the preset's word-scope colour highlight
arrives whatever this pack says about it. Null is how a pack cut
from that preset declines the feature.
There is no `colors.highlight` either - there is no palette here at
all - so nothing draws a swatch row for words that cannot be picked
out (see editor.paletteOf, which hides that row on a channel with
no highlight).
_comment_panel: None, and its absence is half of this channel's design. Written as
null rather than left out, which is the opposite of what
laugh-society-snapchat does and is right for the opposite reason:
that pack inherits nothing, so a key restating the skeleton's own
null would read as a slab somebody had switched off. This one takes
the Snapchat caption preset, and the preset states a card - its
shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow. Null here is what
removes it, and it has to be said out loud.
Why drop it. On Hall of Femme the card and the hairline are one
decision: a 200-weight face over an unknown photograph disappears,
and the slab is what makes that weight a choice rather than a risk.
The two Fitness Story feeds keep the card without needing it, on
the argument that the colour pairing is their look and there is
nowhere else to put it. This feed has no pairing to place - one
colour, no palette - so the card would be a fifth of the frame of
flat colour buying nothing, over pictures the captions exist to
show.
There is no `colors.panel` either, so the swatch row that fills a
card on most of its siblings is not drawn at all rather than drawn
dead (see editor.paletteOf).

_comment_branding: No dark gradient, like every pack under this heading - and like
Conspiracy Central and Crowned Ladies FR this is a channel where the
usual reason does not apply, because its siblings say the gradient has
nothing to do when a title is on a card rather than on the photograph,
and this title IS on the photograph.
It still has nothing to do. The backend's gradient is a SIDE gradient -
full height, never past half the width, peaking on whichever side the
title column is (reframe_engine.apply_dark_gradient) - because it was
drawn for a landscape thumbnail with a headline set beside the subject.
There is no title column on a captured still: the block lies across the
width of the frame, and darkening one half of forty pictures would
shade half of every caption and leave the other half exactly as it was.
No `scrim` either, which is the tool that WOULD reach across the foot
of the frame, and this is the pack under this heading with the best
case for one: Laugh Society throws a scrim and sets white type on it,
and a cream at 0.86 luminance is the same pairing. It is still not
taken. A scrim is a band of shade across the bottom fifth of all forty
pictures whether or not the caption on any given one needed it, which
is the card's cost paid in grey instead of in colour; the drop shadow
buys the same separation one letter at a time and leaves the pictures
whole. If this show ever finds the shadow is not enough, a scrim is the
next thing to try and laugh-society-1 is the pack to read for it.
